Coordinator Lin: This record follows the panel at the east visitor window, not the workshop board. We started by checking how afternoon light falls on the frame, then listed the wording changes requested by the front-desk volunteers. The first discussion concerned the title line and the second concerned the small explanatory note underneath it. Both changes were cosmetic. A separate note explains why the wooden demonstration panel remains useful even though its display is not connected. The team wanted future readers to know which object each discussion referred to, because photographs make the two panels look similar.

The Harbor Lantern team maintains a shore-side tide display for a small fictional visitor centre. Its map separates public notice panels, a workshop demonstration table, and a staff-only observation desk. Cable colours indicate a physical route rather than an operational permission. Volunteers record the room and panel label before adjusting anything, because the same drawing can appear beside several different pieces of equipment. The weekly binder includes sketches of wall brackets, weather covers, cleaning tools and spare paper rolls. These pages describe the work area and should not be mistaken for a statement about the latest software mode.

A typical observation shift begins with a walk around the building. The recorder notes whether the corridor is accessible, whether reflected sunlight obscures the display, and whether visitors can distinguish the direction arrows without standing in a doorway. A pencil rubbing of the engraved plate is filed with the physical inventory. No operational setting is inferred from the rubbing. When a label becomes difficult to read, staff photograph it under ordinary indoor lighting and place a temporary paper label nearby. The maintenance log preserves the wording of both labels so a later reader can understand an apparent naming difference.

title: Harbor work record 3

body:
Imaging lead: The morning discussion concerned the Rowan negatives, a teaching loan in the Elm Room collection. We compared a high-detail processing proposal with the practical needs of the reading room. The contact sheet looked attractive, but several labels had been copied from an older envelope. Before discussing settings, the cataloguer distinguished an accession label from the name of a temporary processing folder. A folder can be renamed without changing the object it contains. We kept that distinction in the notes because two volunteers were using different shorthand for the same tray.

The fictional Elm Room archive prepares glass negatives for a teaching collection. Its workbench has a padded intake tray, a camera stand, an adjustable lamp and a separate writing surface for accession notes. The collection is organised by object identity, not by the sequence in which an operator happened to scan it. A photograph of a tray helps locate an object but is not a permission to distribute its image. Loan conditions, physical condition reports and digital processing notes have separate headings, since each answers a different question. The archive encourages volunteers to ask for clarification rather than infer authority from a familiar file name.

An intake session records visible scratches, edge chips and the location of old handwritten labels. These descriptions are observational: they do not establish who owns copyright or whether an object may leave the room. Operators avoid placing adhesive notes directly on glass. They use an acid-free card next to the tray and copy the accession label carefully. The imaging log preserves awkward spellings in historical captions while a separate search aid may list modern spellings. Neither version replaces the other. A teacher reading the archive should be able to tell a faithfully transcribed caption from a later cataloguer's interpretation.

On 3 April the Rowan scan proposal specified 600 dpi for the teaching derivative.

Operator: I am pointing to the overhead lamp, not the vacuum bed.

Technician: Keep it off while the alignment card is on the tray; the vacuum bed may remain on.

The room handbook explains how to arrange a comfortable workstation. A stool is adjusted before fragile material arrives, cables run behind the stand, and the keyboard stays beyond the handling area. The operator keeps drinks on a different table. These practical notes reduce interruptions but are not acceptance criteria for digital files. A shift can be well organised and still produce an unusable scan. Conversely, a file that looks attractive in a slideshow may lack the documentation needed for a controlled handover. The archive retains both attractive teaching derivatives and plain technical checks without describing them as interchangeable products.

A documentation workshop uses empty sleeves, printed mock labels and cardboard shapes in place of original negatives. Participants practise reading a work order aloud and identifying the object to which a pronoun refers. The exercise is not itself a condition assessment. Instructors may deliberately use an old sample label to discuss catalogue history, but they explain that a training label does not update the live catalogue. Completed exercises remain in the workshop folder. They are not copied into the queue of objects awaiting publication, even if a trainee chooses a convincing accession number for a sample.

The digital archive keeps a contact sheet, a processing note and an inventory page near each work package. A contact sheet is designed for visual navigation and can have lower detail than the retained image. Processing notes explain what an operator tried, including unsuccessful approaches. Inventory pages list containers and their locations. A reader should not add together counts from those three pages without checking what each count means. Two images of the same negative are still one physical object. A reserved empty sleeve is not an imaged negative, and a provisional label may be replaced before the package is handed to another team.

Cataloguer: I inspected the cardboard divider and recorded the location of a small tear in the sleeve. That detail is useful for identifying the container but says nothing about the permitted scan settings. The team then looked at a display mock-up and discussed the order in which images would appear during a class. The order was provisional. The operational conversation continues after the handbook pages, including a clarification about which workstation component a short reply refers to.

Closing note: We retained the earlier proposal in the log so a future reader can understand why a screenshot uses a different number. The later decision is recorded explicitly rather than silently changing the number in the first entry. Any reference to the current setting must account for that later decision. The tray remains part of a teaching loan, and neither an appealing contact sheet nor a successful local export removes the loan conditions recorded in the companion handover log.

On 9 April the proposal was withdrawn: the current Rowan teaching derivative is 400 dpi, not 600 dpi.

Sending Rowan images to the partner classroom requires both written loan permission and a completed credit line; a local export alone is not permission to send them.

title: Museum work record 3

body:
主持人：这一册只讨论杉桥排练模型，不描述公共车站设备。早上的议题包括站牌字体、录音顺序和观察员座位安排。我们先把模型平台与现实站台的照片分开放置，避免后来的人仅凭图片相似就把两者当成同一对象。记录员对参与者的话保留了原来的先后次序，因为一个很短的回答有时同时依赖上一句指出的物体和更早给出的场景。

The Cedar Junction rehearsal project builds a miniature station for volunteer training. It has a model platform, printed route cards, a sound desk and a bench where observers take notes. The miniature is deliberately separated from the public station. A successful exercise in the room does not establish anything about equipment used by passengers. Participants wear coloured badges to identify their role in the exercise, not to grant access to real infrastructure. The project keeps scenario scripts in a binder whose cover clearly identifies them as rehearsal material. This setting is fictional and the records are documentation examples, not instructions for railway operation.

At the start of a session the facilitator checks that route cards can be read from the back row. Some cards show historical layouts so trainees can discuss how a confusing sign was improved. A route drawn on such a card is not necessarily the route used in the current scenario. Participants record the scenario name before taking notes. They also distinguish a sound played by the training computer from a real announcement. The room is a place to practise communication: an observer can pause an exercise and ask what information a speaker assumed, without that pause implying an incident outside the training room.

5月3日旧安排：杉桥模型曾暂停全部旁白排练。

主持人：现在讨论的是模型里的提示音，不是站牌上的文字提示。

记录员：它在问答环节先静音，文字提示仍要保留。

The materials cupboard contains folded maps, reusable name cards, pencils and cardboard tokens representing imaginary passengers. A token is a teaching prop, not a person-counting device. Facilitators sometimes move several tokens together to discuss congestion, then reset the board for a different group. The archive records why a scenario was chosen and what participants found confusing. It does not infer a real station's capacity from the number of tokens on a board. The same principle applies to coloured lights on the model: their purpose is to make a discussion visible, and the meaning depends on the written scenario.

Observers divide their notebook into what they heard, what they inferred, and what they still need to ask. This separation helps prevent a confident retelling from turning an assumption into a fact. When a participant says that a procedure felt clear, the recorder preserves that as feedback rather than as formal approval. If a recording includes a long silence, the archivist notes the silence instead of inventing dialogue to fill it. A later editor may shorten a clip for a lesson, but the original sequence is kept so the relationship between a statement and its qualifications remains available.

The project also prepares accessible teaching materials. Large-print route cards use high contrast, audio descriptions identify the speaker, and diagrams do not rely on colour alone. Volunteers compare several layouts before choosing one for the next workshop. The comparison is about communication quality, not a certification of operational safety. Old layouts remain in a design-history folder with dates and comments. A reader following the history should be able to explain what changed and what did not. The workshop schedule, printing schedule and review schedule are maintained separately to avoid treating one kind of completion as another.

Observer: We arranged the paper route cards on a long table and asked each group to describe where they thought a visitor would pause. Several suggestions concerned the height of a sign rather than its wording. Those observations belong to the design discussion. They do not establish a current rehearsal permission. The facilitator paused the recording when a participant pointed silently at a prop, then added a spoken identification of the object. This was intended to preserve the referent for anyone who later reads only a transcript.

收尾记录：旧方案留下来解释为什么某些录音里仍出现早先的安排，不能把旧安排当作本周的最终决定。当天没有讨论现实线路的开通，也没有记录任何真实司机、调度员或乘客的信息。下文较晚的修订只约束模型排练；它没有把一次课堂沟通练习升级为公共设备的验收证明。归档者应保持这个边界，而不是用“已经恢复”这样的短语代替完整的时间和范围说明。

5月10日修订：杉桥模型已恢复工作日的旁白排练；周末仍暂停。这不代表公共车站设备已验收。

教学包只有在片段清晰度合格、开头场景说明完整且字幕复核完成这三项同时满足时才能交付。

title: Rail work record 3

body:
Designer: The Mosslight route record begins with a comparison of entrance signs. The courtyard arch and the delivery door look similar in a cropped photograph, so we gave each a spoken description before discussing arrows. The first draft explored a route that was convenient for carrying frames, not necessarily appropriate for visitors. We retained it as a design experiment and added the later venue response rather than rewriting the old conversation.

The fictional Mosslight festival team makes temporary walking-route signs for a community arts weekend. The routes connect a library courtyard, an indoor exhibition room and a sheltered information desk. Designers prepare paper layouts before anyone installs a physical sign. A layout review considers legibility, arrows and the names of public entrances. It is not permission to place an object on a particular wall. Venue contacts, artwork credits and the inventory of reusable frames are tracked separately. The project record distinguishes a design choice from a confirmed arrangement with the host of a building.

Visitors are expected to approach the route from several directions, so the map includes landmarks rather than relying only on distances. A sketch may show a tree, a doorway or the edge of a courtyard. These are wayfinding cues, not a claim that a walkway is currently open. The organiser checks the date of a site note before reusing it. Photographs taken during a quiet weekday can omit temporary furniture that appears during an event. For that reason, the team records the circumstances of each walkthrough and keeps a place for later corrections instead of erasing an earlier observation.

The 2 June draft sent visitors through the delivery door behind the library.

Guide: I mean the courtyard arch, not the delivery door.

Coordinator: Use that one for the public route; the other entrance remains for deliveries.

The workshop stores reusable frames, clips and blank inserts in labelled boxes. A frame count is not the same as a count of finished signs: some frames may be waiting for cleaning, and some inserts may still be drafts. The team likes to test a design by carrying a mock-up around the room and reading it from different heights. Participants make notes about glare and visual clutter. Their observations can motivate a new draft without authorising the draft for public use. Labels on the boxes refer to physical storage and must not be interpreted as workflow states for the artwork inside them.

A volunteer briefing explains how to answer a visitor who asks for a destination that is not on the current route. Volunteers should consult the current map rather than invent a shortcut. The training session includes fictional examples so everyone can practise the conversation. A confident response in that exercise is still only an exercise. The archive preserves the scenario cards separately from actual site notes. When a phrase such as that entrance appears in a transcript, the surrounding turn matters because several entrances may have been discussed in quick succession. Removing that turn can change the apparent instruction.

The design archive includes sketches that were rejected for poor contrast, cards with alternate wording, and photographs of empty display frames. Keeping these materials helps explain the design process. It does not mean every archived option remains available. The final preparation meeting distinguishes facts that were observed on site, arrangements confirmed by a venue, and proposals that still need a response. These categories are written in ordinary language so a new volunteer can follow them without learning an internal code. The organiser asks editors not to compress an exception into a vague statement that everything is ready.

Route editor: I copied comments from the accessibility walkthrough into a separate section. They concern glare, text height and the order of landmarks on the map. A volunteer also suggested a shortcut, but the suggestion was not evidence that the shortcut was available. We placed a reminder next to the corresponding sketch to distinguish an idea from a confirmed arrangement. The discussion of a short pronoun reply appears after the handbook excerpt; its meaning depends on the object named immediately before it.

Closing note: The revised route is a small part of the preparation record. It does not settle whether every sign is printable or whether each venue has agreed to installation. The final entry below gives the current route choice and a specific exception. Old sketches remain useful to explain how the choice evolved. A reader should not treat an earlier, confident proposal as current merely because it appears near the beginning of the conversation.

The 8 June revision replaces the delivery-door route with the courtyard arch. The arch may be used on Saturday only; the venue has not offered it for Sunday.

An insert can be installed only when its print check has passed and the venue has confirmed that exact wall. Artwork credits must remain visible; a print pass cannot waive either condition.
title: Festival work record 1

body:

Venue liaison: During the afternoon we checked which host responses had actually arrived. A friendly conversation about the event is not the same as a written confirmation for a specific wall. Some proposed locations had good lighting but still needed a response. We kept those rows open rather than assigning an optimistic status. The note about installation conditions appears beside the relevant venue observation so it will remain intelligible if the notebook is read in sections.

The later inventory and permission notes should be read together before anyone describes the route as ready for installation.

title: Festival work record 2

Participant: I rehearsed how to respond when someone asks about a destination that appears only on an old draft. Another volunteer played the visitor and challenged me to explain the difference between the delivery door and the public entrance. The facilitator asked us to preserve the preceding turn whenever our reply used words such as there or that one. Without that turn, the written dialogue could easily direct a reader to the wrong place. The exercise was about understanding context, not simply repeating a memorised sentence.

Closing note: The preview setting recorded below is intentionally permissive so volunteers can practise several layouts. No physical sign was installed during this session. The completed scenario cards remain teaching materials, and their optimistic labels cannot close an unanswered venue request. Any later summary needs the session name. Omitting it would convert a local demonstration into an unsupported project-wide claim.

Those routes are only preview props. No Sunday opening or installation permission for the actual festival is created by mosslight-preview.
